Anabaptism
an-uh-BAP-tiz-um
noun
From Greek ana- (again) + baptizein (to dip, to baptize) + -ism (doctrine, practice). The term was coined pejoratively by Reformers and Catholics alike to describe those who “rebaptized” adults previously baptized as infants—a charge the movement itself rejected, arguing that infant baptism was no baptism at all.

Biblical Definition

Anabaptism refers to the 16th-century Radical Reformation movement that distinguished itself from both Roman Catholicism and the magisterial Reformation by insisting upon believers' baptism (credobaptism), the voluntary gathered church, the separation of church and state, and rigorous discipleship standards. The name Anabaptist—rebaptizer—was applied externally; the movement's own leaders argued they were not re-baptizing but baptizing for the first time those who had received only an empty rite in infancy. Theologically, Anabaptism grounded baptism in conscious repentance and faith (Acts 2:38; Matt. 28:19), holding that the covenant community is constituted by regenerate members who publicly profess Christ rather than by geographic or national Christendom. The movement included Zwinglian-influenced Swiss Brethren (Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz), south German figures (Balthasar Hübmaier, who accepted magisterial authority more than most), and Mennonite streams (Menno Simons). Anabaptism ranged from the orthodox (Schleitheim Confession, 1527) to the heterodox (Thomas Müntzer's political radicalism, the Münster commune). Historians of the Reformation rightly distinguish the mainstream Anabaptists, who were peaceable credobaptists, from the violent millenarian fringe. The Schleitheim tradition directly influenced later Baptist ecclesiology and the Free Church tradition. Evaluation must be nuanced: Anabaptist baptismal theology and its insistence on regenerate church membership align with 1689 Baptist convictions even where Anabaptist pacifism and two-kingdoms separatism diverge from confessional Reformed thought.

Webster 1828 Definition

Anabaptist: one of a sect that arose in Germany about 1521, who rejected infant baptism as invalid and administered baptism anew to adults; also called Re-baptizers.

expand to see more

AN-A-BAP'TIST, noun. One of a sect who maintain that baptism ought always to be performed by immersion.

2. (Historical) One who denies the validity of infant baptism and insists on re-baptizing adults—a position common in Germany in the 16th century that spread to England and America.

3. The name was originally a term of reproach applied by opponents; the party themselves denied that they were re-baptizing, since they held infant baptism to be no baptism.

AN-A-BAP'TISM, noun. The doctrine or practice of the Anabaptists; rejection of infant baptism and insistence on adult or believers' baptism.

The term and the movement must be distinguished from the violent millenarian fringe (Münster, 1534–35) which the mainstream Anabaptists repudiated.

Key Scripture

Matthew 28:19 — "Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,"

Romans 6:3 — "Or don't you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?"

Romans 6:4 — "We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life."

Colossians 2:12 — "having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead."

Modern Corruption

Post-liberal scholarship domesticates Anabaptism into a proto-pacifist social-justice movement, stripping its baptismal theology and harvesting only its anti-Christendom politics for contemporary progressive agendas.

expand to see more

The contemporary misappropriation operates on two fronts. Academic “neo-Anabaptist” writers (Yoder, Hauerwas) amplify the separatist and pacifist dimensions while quietly shelving the credobaptist ecclesiology that defined the movement—the result is an “Anabaptism” that can feel at home in liberal Protestant denominations that practice infant baptism and celebrate progressive sexuality. On the popular level, online circles invoke Anabaptist simplicity and community as an aesthetic escape from institutional church, divorced from the movement's rigorous discipline and confessional accountability.

The recovery requires holding together what the Schleitheim Anabaptists themselves held together: believers' baptism, regenerate church membership, congregational accountability, and separation from worldly corruption—not merely from state power but from theological compromise. The 1689 London Baptist Confession stands in direct theological lineage with the confessional Anabaptist streams while correcting the Two-Kingdoms separatism and pacifism that Scripture does not require. To reclaim Anabaptism is to reclaim the gathered, covenanted, baptizing church—not a romantic anti-institutional spirituality.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ana- + baptizein reveals the movement's defining claim: that true baptism follows true faith, making infant rites no rite at all.

expand to see more

Greek ana- — again, anew, back; the prefix that gave the movement its name and its enemies their charge of “re-baptizing”

Greek baptizein — to dip, immerse, wash; the act that joins the believer to Christ's death and resurrection (Rom. 6:3–4)

Latin -ismus — a doctrinal system or practice, pointing to the movement's theological coherence beyond mere ritual preference

German Wiedertäufer — re-baptizers, the German term of reproach; the Swiss Brethren called themselves simply Brüder (brothers)

Latin credere (to believe) — root of credobaptism, the positive term for the conviction that personal faith precedes and grounds baptism

Usage

"Distinguishing the confessional Anabaptist mainstream (Schleitheim, Menno Simons) from the violent Münster radicals is essential to honest historical and theological assessment."

"The 1689 Baptist Confession represents a Reformed correction and confessionalization of the credobaptist instinct the Anabaptists held, preserving what Scripture requires while anchoring it in Reformed soteriology."

"Neo-Anabaptist social ethics, divorced from credobaptist ecclesiology and confessional discipline, should be treated as a distinct modern construct rather than a recovery of the 16th-century movement."
